correctness.rationale: For each positive terminal cap, the exact transformation z_x=d_G(u,x)-f(x), s=L-f(v) has absolute Jacobian one. Geodesic orientation gives 0<=z_b-z_a<=2ell_ab; directed u-v paths force z_x in [0,s], and the cap bound s<=2ell_min eliminates upper constraints. The slice is s times the reachability order polytope, volume s^(N-2)e(P)/(N-2)! by its elementary simplex triangulation. Integrating and doubling yields 2e(P)epsilon^(N-1)/(N-1)!. The height-two graph is bipartite of diameter exactly three and preserves order, and a factorial multiplier recovers the #P-complete extension count. Fourteen exact lattice-point/Ehrhart examples test representative boundaries but do not substitute for proof.

originality.rationale: An order-polytope/linear-extension volume identity and restricted poset counting hardness are known separately. The combined finding specifies a symmetric graph-metric Lipschitz-dual terminal-edge response for arbitrary terminal geodesic networks and uses an explicit unweighted bipartite diameter-three embedding to transfer restricted #P-hardness. The formerly obtained complete-bipartite edge formula is a special case and is credited, not claimed new. The inspected references do not assert this same theorem; risk of equivalent unindexed or alternate-formulation coverage remains.
residual_risks: The equivalence between some poset hypersimplex descriptions and certain metric caps may be implicit in other literature not retrieved; this prevents a uniqueness claim, not an assertion of known coverage.

value.rationale: The volume response for an infinite class of natural metric-space Banach dual balls is exactly controlled by the linear-extension count of a terminal-geodesic reachability order. The polynomial-time reduction proves exact evaluation #P-hard already for a sharply restricted class of unweighted bipartite diameter-three base graphs, providing a concrete computational-complexity barrier of use in choosing exact versus approximate methods. This is not an arbitrary small sample or a mere recomputation of a known order-polytope volume.
